3.x: Four key elements structure this section: localisation, quality, distribution and triggers. The course lists six questions: 1. Are there trophic disorders — lower limb, vulva, vagina? Very dry skin on the foot, eschars. 2. Is there numbness or loss of sensation? Ask directly: "when I touch this area, do you feel my 6nger or do you feel numbness?". Loss of sensation suggests a neurogenic lesion; if touching hurts more, that is hyperaesthesia and suggests irritation. 3. Is there dysaesthesia or neuropathic phantom pain? 4. Is the numbness ascending or descending? That pattern suggests polyneuropathy. 5. Is temperature sensation altered, cold or warm? 6. Are there sensory changes during micturition, defecation or intercourse? the distribution; abnormalities such as burning and dysaesthesia. Course slide (© ISNP). The manual adds the rule of thumb: extrinsic lesions that merely irritate the nerve do not cause loss of sensation or numbness, whereas neurogenic damage is accompanied by loss of sensation in the corresponding distribution. The distal 6xation, to the vagina, lies between both inferior hypogastric plexuses: if the pain comes from there it will be visceral. The proximal 6xation, to the promontorium, exposes the S2 root and sometimes S3: if the pain comes from there it will be somatic — burning perianal pain plus dorsal and medial thigh sciatica. Determining which of the two is the origin is the key to management. RULE In secondary entrapment, never remove the mesh and never resect the Gbrosis: release the nerve. 3.x: the right, its relation to Alcock's canal. Course slide (© ISNP). When the condition is attributed to the episiotomy, the course proposes 6ve questions: is the pain vulvar, perineal or perianal? Is there a loss-of-genital- sensation syndrome ("loss penis syndrome" in men)? Is there vaginal or vulvar numbness? Is the incontinence urinary or faecal? Is it primary or secondary? Incontinence deserves an anatomical note: urinary incontinence requires a bilateral lesion of the pudendal nerve or of the dorsal nerve of the clitoris. As long as the contralateral side is intact, there will be no incontinence. CAESAREAN SECTION "Pudendal" pain aJer a caesarean section is usually not pudendal: it corresponds to the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve. The patient develops anterior vulvodynia — not the whole vulva — without perineal or perianal pain, and with ascending radiation along the genitofemoral nerve rather than descending. How the neuropelveological diagnosis is built The history builds the diagnosis; the clinical examination confirms it and determines whether the neuropathy is neurogenic or not [Slide Neuropelveologic Diagnosis] [Class]. The diagnosis is not “endometriosis” or “myoma”: it is the name of the nerve and what is wrong with it [Class]. Exam trap. Both conditions are “vascular”, but pelvic congestion causes visceral pain and entrapment causes somatic pain. Pain that goes down the leg every period is somatic: it cannot be pelvic congestion [Class]. Nuance: parasympathetic is not “vegetative”. The pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic autonomic nerves supplying bladder, rectum and uterus: their irritation causes the need to go to the toilet very often, but not the vegetative symptoms (pallor, mydriasis, sweating), which belong to the sympathetic system and are everywhere in the body. 4.x: Unilateral swelling: venous obstruction, lymphedema or DVT; compare both legs at ankle, calf and thigh [Slide]. Skin and nails: trophic changes, ulceration, discoloration, nail dystrophy → chronic ischemia or microvascular disease; associated with vascular or connective tissue disease (EDS, vasculitis) [Slide]. These tests are non-invasive, quick and also useful for follow-up [Slide]. Why the neurogenic leg is warmer Possover explained it in the part that was missing [Class, 0:55]: 1. The sciatic nerve carries sympathetic fibers. 2. Active sympathetic fibers cause vasoconstriction. 3. If the sciatic nerve is destroyed, its sympathetic fibers are destroyed too → peripheral vasodilation → the leg becomes warmer. 4. The same happens when the sympathetic trunk is injured during a para-aortic lymphadenectomy (consistent with the book, ch. I §4.2). Key fact. A difference of 2–3 °C between the legs indicates a problem. Example from the class video: endometriosis of the right sciatic nerve, right foot 28 °C vs left 26 °C. Because the sympathetic fibers inside the nerve were destroyed, Possover knew before surgery that he would have to open or partially resect the sciatic nerve: “in neurope

Surgical warning. These patients have “tricky vessels”: they easily develop thrombosis and pressure sores. Do not compress the external iliac vessels for a long time; Possover knows of patients who lost a leg after hours of compression during robotic surgery [Class]. Why not look at the MRI first “If you’re not sure… in neuropelveology always look at the MRI at the end of the consultation, not at the start” [Class]. What separates these conditions is clinical: diameter, temperature, shoe, strength. 7. Vascular phenotypes and Ehlers-Danlos Vascular entrapment is the number one cause of non-neurogenic pelvic radiculopathy and neuropathy, “by far”, well ahead of nerve endometriosis or surgical injury. And Ehlers-Danlos is the number one cause of vascular entrapment: in a series of 280 patients submitted for publication, 80% had EDS [Class]. Key fact · the vessel is in the wrong place, not huge. Typical example: the superior gluteal vessels normally run between the bone and the nerve; in EDS they run in front of the lumbosacral trunk and compress it against the bone [Class]. That is why in more than 90% of entrapments MRI does not show a large vein [Class]. Own diagram · EDS mechanism

Own diagram · pudendal pain algorithm [Class] [Book, II §2.3, Tab. 2.4; IV §4] How to read it 1. Cannot tolerate sitting (immediate pain), relieved on the toilet seat, standing or lying down → Alcock [Book, Tab. 2.4 and §3.3]. Tolerates sitting → the pudendal nerve is involved above the pelvic floor [Class]. 3. Vascular, endometriosis or pelvic congestion The big question in the closing Q&A: “is it the endometriosis or the vascular entrapment?”. Main difference: vascular pain decreases in every situation that lowers venous pressure (lying down); sciatic endometriosis does not improve at night [Class].

Own diagram · vascular vs endometriosis vs congestion [Class] [Book, Tab. 2.4] All three often coexist. Endometriosis induces neoangiogenesis, and after several pelvic surgeries congestion is frequent: “even removing a tubal vein changes the blood flow in the pelvis” [Class]. The key is always the diagnosis: visceral or somatic? 11.1 The 3 locations of vascular entrapment # Where What it causes 1 Sacral plexus S2–S4, infracardinal portion Sacral radiculopathy: pudendal + buttock/leg, bladder 2 Lumbosacral trunk L5–S1 (atypical superior L5–S1 radiculopathy: low back, buttock, gluteal vessels) dorsal/lateral leg 3 Pudendal at the lesser sciatic foramen Incomplete pudendal pain Source: [Class] (consistent with the book, ch. Compression by an artery (e.g., of the sciatic nerve at the greater sciatic foramen) can cause partial neuropathic damage [Class]. May-Thurner is always left-sided. Possover has seen patients who underwent laparoscopic decompression on the right for suspected May-Thurner: a mistake. Sciatica algorithm Pelvic irritation of the sciatic nerve causes allodynia only in the sacral dermatomes (buttock and dorsal leg). In disc herniation, dorsal and ventral pain combine; bilateral pain points to a spinal or central cause [Book, II §2.3]. Own diagram · sciatica algorithm [Book, II §1, §2.3] [Class] Additional clues Sciatica + urinary symptoms (urgency, frequency, dysuria) without a clear orthopedic cause → think of the sacral plexus [Book, II §1]. Cyclic L5–S1 sciatica → sciatic endometriosis, isolated form [Book, Tab. 2.4]; often causes foot drop and steppage gait [Class]. Pain going down the leg every period → somatic: not pelvic congestion [Class]. Simultaneous bilateral pain with a vascular pattern → don’t forget tricuspid insufficiency (raises IVC pressure) [Class]. See Discrepancies: the book links “bilateral” to a spinal or central cause.
